PoSTCache: From Forecasting to Postdictive Smoothing for Revisable Diffusion Caching

Liwei Lan Email: llw25@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn    Hui Chen Affiliation: School of Software, Tsinghua University  BNRist, Tsinghua University Email: huichen@mail.tsinghua.edu.cn    Jungong Han Affiliation: Department of Automation, Tsinghua University Email: jghan@tsinghua.edu.cn    Guiguang Ding Email: dinggg@tsinghua.edu.cn
Abstract

Diffusion and flow matching models achieve impressive visual generation quality but remain computationally expensive due to iterative sampling. Caching-based acceleration provides a practical training-free solution by reusing or predicting intermediate features. However, existing methods largely enforce a forward-only information flow: approximations produced for skipped model evaluations are immediately committed to the sampling trajectory and cannot benefit from feedback generated by later full-computation steps. We propose PoSTCache (Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache), a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching as revisable trajectory inference. PoSTCache first uses an existing caching strategy to construct forward proposals for skipped steps. At a later full-computation step, the discrepancy between the refreshed prediction and its forward proposal yields a correction signal, which PoSTCache propagates backward to refine and reintegrate the preceding predictions. Viewing full-computation steps as sources of corrective feedback also changes how they should be selected. We therefore introduce the Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) strategy, which estimates cross-timestep dependencies from offline denoising trajectories and selects anchors according to their expected reduction in surrogate trajectory uncertainty rather than local approximation error alone. Experiments on representative image and video generation models show that PoSTCache consistently improves the quality–efficiency trade-off over representative caching methods.

1 Introduction

Diffusion models (Song and Ermon, 2019; Ho et al., 2020; Song et al., 2020b) and flow matching models (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023) have become a dominant paradigm for modern visual generation. By progressively transporting noisy latent variables toward structured data samples, they enable impressive image (Rombach et al., 2022; Podell et al., 2024) and video synthesis quality (Blattmann et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024a). Despite this progress, sampling still requires tens to hundreds of steps, making user-facing applications latency-bound.

Traditional acceleration techniques, such as distillation (Song et al., 2023) and post-training quantization (Li et al., 2023), often incur additional training costs, architectural modifications, or non-trivial deployment efforts. In contrast, caching provides a lightweight, training-free alternative by exploiting the temporal redundancy of intermediate representations (Liu et al., 2025a; Bu et al., 2025; Chung et al., 2026). Existing caching approaches have evolved from static feature reuse (Selvaraju et al., 2024) to adaptive strategies that estimate inter-step redundancy online (Liu et al., 2025a; Ma et al., 2026; Haghighi and Alahi, 2026), extrapolate future feature trajectories with polynomial approximations (Liu et al., 2025b; Feng et al., 2026), or exploit shallow-layer dynamics to guide deep-layer feature reuse (Bu et al., 2025). More recently, caching has also been extended beyond the original feature space to spectral representations (Chung et al., 2026).

Despite their diversity, most existing caching methods follow a strictly forward information flow, which we refer to as forecasting: skipped-step predictions are constructed from historical information and committed to the sampling trajectory without later revision, allowing approximation errors to propagate through subsequent updates, as illustrated in Figure 1(a). This raises a broader question: does later sampling reveal new information that could help correct these earlier errors? In particular, periodic full-computation steps produce fresh predictions after the trajectory has evolved through preceding approximations, potentially exposing backward-looking information about accumulated errors. For example, the discrepancy between a refreshed prediction and its forward proposal can provide such corrective evidence. However, most existing methods use this newly revealed information only for subsequent sampling, rather than propagating it backward to revise earlier estimates. This motivates a postdictive smoothing view of diffusion caching, inspired by Bayesian smoothing, in which later evidence retrospectively revises uncertain intermediate estimates (Rauch et al., 1965; Rabiner, 1989; Särkkä and Svensson, 2023). Accordingly, we treat skipped predictions as provisional rather than final, allowing feedback from later full-computation steps to retrospectively refine these estimates and enable backward information flow, as illustrated in Figure 1(b).

Motivated by this perspective, we propose PoSTCache, short for Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache, a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates cache-based acceleration as revisable trajectory inference. Building on an existing caching strategy, PoSTCache propagates feedback from subsequent full-computation anchors backward to refine skipped predictions and reintegrates the corrected trajectory. This shift also changes how anchors should be valued: from their local approximation error to their trajectory-level corrective value. We therefore introduce the Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) strategy, which estimates cross-timestep dependencies from offline denoising trajectories and greedily selects anchors to reduce surrogate trajectory uncertainty under a fixed computation budget. Figure 1(c) previews the resulting quality–latency trade-off.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    From Forecasting to Postdictive Smoothing. We propose PoSTCache, a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching from forward-only forecasting into postdictive smoothing by retrospectively revising skipped predictions.

  • •

    Posterior Variance Reduction (PVR) Anchor Selection. We propose a smoothing-aware PVR strategy that profiles offline denoising trajectories and greedily selects anchors to reduce surrogate trajectory uncertainty under a fixed computation budget.

  • •

    Superior Performance. Comprehensive experiments across representative image and video models show that PoSTCache improves reconstruction fidelity at comparable or higher acceleration while maintaining competitive semantic generation quality.

2 Related Work

Generative Model Acceleration. Acceleration methods for diffusion and flow-based models reduce either the cost of each model evaluation or the number of sampling steps. The former includes model compression techniques such as pruning (Fang et al., 2023), quantization (Li et al., 2023), and knowledge distillation (Meng et al., 2023), as well as computation-efficient designs such as FlashAttention (Dao et al., 2022) and token reduction (Bolya et al., 2022). The latter improves sampling efficiency through deterministic sampling with DDIM (Song et al., 2020a), high-order ODE solvers such as DPM-Solver (Lu et al., 2022), alternative generative dynamics including flow matching (Lipman et al., 2023) and rectified flow (Liu et al., 2023), or few-step generation through progressive distillation (Salimans and Ho, 2022), consistency models (Song et al., 2023), Shortcut Models (Frans et al., 2025), and MeanFlow (Geng et al., 2026). Although effective, these approaches often require additional training, architectural changes, or modifications to the sampling process.

Cache-based Acceleration. Caching provides a lightweight and training-free alternative by exploiting the temporal redundancy of intermediate representations. Early methods reuse U-Net features with fixed schedules, including DeepCache (Ma et al., 2024) and FasterDiffusion (Li et al., 2024), while FORA (Selvaraju et al., 2024) and Δ\Delta-DiT (Chen et al., 2024b) extend feature or attention reuse to diffusion transformers. More recent approaches adaptively determine when to refresh cached features using different error proxies, such as TeaCache (Liu et al., 2025a), MagCache (Ma et al., 2026), and DiCache (Bu et al., 2025). TaylorSeer (Liu et al., 2025b) and HiCache (Feng et al., 2026) instead predict future features from historical states. Other methods incorporate trajectory priors, including spectral evolution in SeaCache (Chung et al., 2026), global path planning in DPCache (Cui et al., 2026), average-velocity stability in MeanCache (Gao et al., 2026), and offline residual rectification in ERTACache (Peng et al., 2026). Despite these advances, most methods remain online forward-only: skipped states are determined using historical information or offline priors and remain unrevised after future full-computation states become available.

Bayesian Posterior Smoothing. Bayesian smoothing estimates an intermediate latent state using both past and future observations, whereas filtering conditions only on observations available up to the current time. For linear Gaussian systems, this principle underlies Kalman filtering (Kalman, 1960) and the Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoother (Rauch et al., 1965). A similar forward–backward inference procedure is used in hidden Markov models (Rabiner, 1989). Bayesian smoothing has been generalized to nonlinear and non-Gaussian state-space models (Särkkä and Svensson, 2023). These methods share the central idea that future evidence can retrospectively correct uncertain intermediate estimates, motivating our reformulation of diffusion caching as revisable trajectory inference.

3 Method

3.1 Preliminaries

Diffusion sampling evolves a latent trajectory through a sequence of model predictions and state updates, resembling sequential Bayesian estimation (Kalman, 1960). At each denoising step, the model produces a prediction from the information available so far, which is then used by the numerical solver to advance the trajectory. When some predictions are replaced by inaccurate approximations, their errors can propagate through subsequent updates and accumulate along the trajectory.

Bayesian smoothing provides a principled mechanism for revising such forward estimates once informative future evidence becomes available (Rauch et al., 1965; Rabiner, 1989; Särkkä and Svensson, 2023). Under a linear Gaussian approximation, conditioning the forward estimate at step tt on an observation at a later step bb gives

mt|b=mt+Pt​b​(Pb​b+Rb)−1​(yb−mb),m_{t\mid b}=m_{t}+P_{tb}(P_{bb}+R_{b})^{-1}(y_{b}-m_{b}), (1)

where yb−mby_{b}-m_{b} is the future innovation, defined as the residual between the future observation yby_{b} and its forward prediction mbm_{b}. The factor Pt​b​(Pb​b+Rb)−1P_{tb}(P_{bb}+R_{b})^{-1} is the smoothing gain. The conditional mean, therefore, takes the generic form

smoothed estimate=forward estimate+smoothing gain×future innovation.\text{smoothed estimate}=\text{forward estimate}+\text{smoothing gain}\times\text{future innovation}. (2)

This perspective motivates treating skipped diffusion predictions as revisable forward estimates rather than fixed approximations. The sequential-estimation interpretation and the corresponding smoothing derivation are provided in Appendices A.1 and A.2, respectively.

3.2 Trajectory Analysis

Existing caching methods construct skipped predictions from historical states, whose approximation errors are integrated into the sampling trajectory and remain unrevised. We investigate whether a later full-computation step provides useful evidence for retrospectively correcting these errors.

Consider a cache interval bounded by two full-computation steps a<ba<b. Let u~k\widetilde{u}_{k} and u¯k\bar{u}_{k} denote the cached and full-computation predictions at step kk, respectively. We define

ek=u¯k−u~k,rb=u¯b−u~b,a<k<b,e_{k}=\bar{u}_{k}-\widetilde{u}_{k},\qquad r_{b}=\bar{u}_{b}-\widetilde{u}_{b},\quad a<k<b, (3)

where eke_{k} is the proposal error, and rbr_{b} is the future-anchor residual. Following the Bayesian smoothing interpretation in Sec. 3.1, we hereafter refer to this residual as the anchor innovation.

Future anchors provide corrective information.

Figure 2(a) shows that eke_{k} and rbr_{b} are consistently positively aligned, with stronger alignment as the intermediate step approaches the future anchor. Across interval lengths from 55 to 1010, the relative position ρk=(k−a)/(b−a)\rho_{k}=(k-a)/(b-a) and the cosine alignment cos⁡(ek,rb)\cos(e_{k},r_{b}) exhibit pooled Spearman correlations of 0.980.98 on both Qwen-Image-2512 and Wan 2.1. Moreover, the mean alignment at near-anchor positions (ρk≥0.75\rho_{k}\geq 0.75) exceeds that at far-anchor positions (ρk≤0.25\rho_{k}\leq 0.25) by 0.350.35 and 0.360.36, respectively. These results indicate that the anchor innovation rbr_{b} contains increasingly accurate directional information about the errors accumulated within the preceding interval.

Figure 2(b) measures the fraction of proposal error removed by a scalar correction:

EERk,b⁡(g)=1−‖ek−g​rb‖22‖ek‖22.\operatorname{EER}_{k,b}(g)=1-\frac{\|e_{k}-gr_{b}\|_{2}^{2}}{\|e_{k}\|_{2}^{2}}. (4)

We compare the oracle scalar gain gk,boracle=arg⁡ming⁡‖ek−g​rb‖22g_{k,b}^{\mathrm{oracle}}=\arg\min_{g}\|e_{k}-gr_{b}\|_{2}^{2} with the relative-position gain gk,blinear=ρkg_{k,b}^{\mathrm{linear}}=\rho_{k}. Despite requiring no sample-specific estimation, the linear gain retains 96.3%96.3\% and 97.0%97.0\% of the oracle explained error on Qwen-Image-2512 and Wan 2.1, with mean EER gaps of only 0.0470.047 and 0.0190.019, respectively. This shows that sampling progress provides a simple approximation to the oracle scalar correction strength, motivating our time-dependent smoothing gain.

Local error is a poor proxy for anchor informativeness.

Figure 2(c) compares local cache risk with trajectory-level correction value (Appendix C.1). The two criteria are poorly aligned: their pooled Spearman correlations are negative, with 0%0\% top-11 agreement and median regrets of 39.1%39.1\% and 47.9%47.9\% on Qwen-Image-2512 and Wan 2.1, respectively. Therefore, the step with the largest local error is not necessarily the most informative anchor for correcting the preceding trajectory.

3.3 PoSTCache

Motivated by the Bayesian smoothing principle in Sec. 3.1, which revises a forward estimate using a gain-weighted anchor innovation, and supported by the empirical observations in Sec. 3.2, PoSTCache uses future-anchor innovations for retrospective trajectory correction and trajectory-level uncertainty for anchor selection, as shown in Figure 3.

3.3.1 Postdictive Smoothing Trajectory Cache

Let uk=fθ​(xk,τk)u_{k}=f_{\theta}(x_{k},\tau_{k}) denote the model prediction consumed by the numerical solver at the kk-th denoising step. Consider two consecutive full-computation anchors a<ba<b. Starting from anchor aa, an existing caching method constructs forward proposals for the intermediate predictions:

u~k=𝒫k(ℋa),k=a+1,…,b,\widetilde{u}_{k}=\mathcal{P}_{k}(\mathcal{H}_{a}),\qquad k=a+1,\ldots,b, (5)

where ℋa\mathcal{H}_{a} contains the historical states available at anchor aa, and 𝒫k\mathcal{P}_{k} can represent feature reuse, extrapolation, or other forward caching strategies. In our default implementation, 𝒫k\mathcal{P}_{k} simply reuses the latest full-computation prediction.

At the next anchor bb, a full model evaluation produces u¯b\bar{u}_{b}. The resulting anchor residual is

rb=u¯b−u~b,r_{b}=\bar{u}_{b}-\widetilde{u}_{b}, (6)

where u~b\widetilde{u}_{b} is the corresponding forward proposal. As established in Sec. 3.2, this residual is the anchor innovation used in the following smoothing update.

Under a local linear Gaussian approximation of the proposal errors, conditioning the intermediate proposal on the future anchor innovation yields

u^k=u~k+Gk←b​(u¯b−u~b),\widehat{u}_{k}=\widetilde{u}_{k}+G_{k\leftarrow b}\left(\bar{u}_{b}-\widetilde{u}_{b}\right), (7)

where Gk←bG_{k\leftarrow b} is a covariance-dependent smoothing gain that propagates the anchor innovation backward to step kk. It assigns stronger corrections when the intermediate proposal error is more closely correlated with the anchor innovation, while accounting for the uncertainty of the future evidence. This conditioning also reduces the remaining uncertainty of the intermediate prediction. The detailed forms of the smoothing gain and posterior covariance are provided in Appendix A.3.

Although computing the full high-dimensional gain is impractical, the analysis in Sec. 3.2 shows that a simple relative-position scalar gain captures most of the oracle scalar correction. We therefore adopt the lightweight isotropic approximation Gk←b≈wk|a,b​IG_{k\leftarrow b}\approx w_{k\mid a,b}I, giving

u^k=u~k+wk|a,b​(u¯b−u~b),wk|a,b=ηk−ηaηb−ηa,a<k≤b,\widehat{u}_{k}=\widetilde{u}_{k}+w_{k\mid a,b}\left(\bar{u}_{b}-\widetilde{u}_{b}\right),\qquad w_{k\mid a,b}=\frac{\eta_{k}-\eta_{a}}{\eta_{b}-\eta_{a}},\quad a<k\leq b, (8)

where ηk\eta_{k} denotes the sampling progress, instantiated by the step index. The resulting gain increases from 00 to 11 across the interval, gradually incorporating the future evidence.

Correcting the model predictions alone does not revise the latent states already produced within the skipped interval. We therefore reintegrate the corrected predictions from anchor aa:

x^k+1=𝒮k​(x^k,u^k,τk),x^a=xa,\widehat{x}_{k+1}=\mathcal{S}_{k}\left(\widehat{x}_{k},\widehat{u}_{k},\tau_{k}\right),\qquad\widehat{x}_{a}=x_{a}, (9)

where 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k} is the original scheduler or numerical solver. Reintegration involves only inexpensive solver operations and requires no additional neural-network evaluations at skipped steps; for efficiency, we also retain the already-computed future-anchor prediction u¯b\bar{u}_{b} rather than re-evaluating the model at the reintegrated anchor state x^b\widehat{x}_{b}. We further examine the resulting anchor-state consistency and its compute trade-off in Appendix C.6.

3.3.2 Posterior Variance Reduction Anchor Selection

The analysis in Sec. 3.2 shows that local cache risk does not reliably reflect the trajectory-level correction value required for effective postdictive smoothing. Since directly modeling proposal errors requires costly rollouts and depends on the proposal method, cache interval, and caching configuration, we instead profile NN complete offline denoising trajectories to construct a proposal-agnostic surrogate. Let zk(n)=u¯k(n)∈ℝDz_{k}^{(n)}=\bar{u}_{k}^{(n)}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denote the full-computation model prediction at timestep kk for the nn-th sample. We construct the timestep-level covariance kernel

μk=1N​∑n=1Nzk(n),Ki​j=1N​D​∑n=1N⟨zi(n)−μi,zj(n)−μj⟩,\mu_{k}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}z_{k}^{(n)},\qquad K_{ij}=\frac{1}{ND}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle z_{i}^{(n)}-\mu_{i},\,z_{j}^{(n)}-\mu_{j}\right\rangle, (10)

where Ki​jK_{ij} summarizes the normalized cross-timestep covariance. A large magnitude |Ki​j||K_{ij}| indicates a strong dependency between trajectory states at timesteps ii and jj.

Using KK as a covariance model, the posterior variance at step tt conditioned on an anchor set AA is

Vt​(A)=Kt​t−Kt​A​KA​A−1​KA​t.V_{t}(A)=K_{tt}-K_{tA}K_{AA}^{-1}K_{At}. (11)

Given a computation budget ℬ\mathcal{B}, we select anchors by minimizing the weighted trajectory uncertainty:

A⋆=arg⁡min⁡∑t=1TA0⊆A|A|≤ℬ⁡γt​Vt​(A),A^{\star}=\arg\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}A_{0}\subseteq A\\ |A|\leq\mathcal{B}\end{subarray}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma_{t}V_{t}(A), (12)

where A0A_{0} contains the dense-prefix anchors and the final denoising step, and γt\gamma_{t} is a scheduler-aware temporal weight. Detailed implementation settings are provided in Appendix B.2.

Since exact optimization is combinatorial, we greedily select the candidate with the largest marginal variance reduction. Given the current anchor set AA, we define the conditional cross-covariance

Ct​s|A=Kt​s−Kt​A​KA​A−1​KA​s.C_{ts\mid A}=K_{ts}-K_{tA}K_{AA}^{-1}K_{As}. (13)

Under Gaussian conditioning, adding candidate ss reduces the posterior variance at timestep tt by Ct​s|A 2/Vs​(A)C_{ts\mid A}^{\,2}/V_{s}(A). Its weighted marginal gain over the trajectory is therefore

Δ⁡(s∣A)=∑t=1Tγt​Ct​s|A 2Vs​(A),s⋆=arg⁡maxs∉A⁡Δ⁡(s∣A).\Delta(s\mid A)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma_{t}\frac{C_{ts\mid A}^{\,2}}{V_{s}(A)},\qquad s^{\star}=\arg\max_{s\notin A}\Delta(s\mid A). (14)

This criterion favors anchors with high trajectory-level correction value rather than large local variation alone. Appendix A.4 derives it as posterior variance reduction under the linear Gaussian surrogate, while Appendix C.3 validates this surrogate on held-out trajectories, showing strong correlation with measured post-smoothing error (ρ=0.858/0.963\rho=0.858/0.963 on Qwen-Image/Wan).

4 Experiments

4.1 Settings

Base Models and Compared Methods. We evaluate PoSTCache on three video generation models, Open-Sora 1.2 (Zheng et al., 2024), CogVideoX (Yang et al., 2025), and Wan 2.1 (Wan et al., 2025), and two image generation models, FLUX.1-dev (Labs, 2024) and Qwen-Image-2512 (Wu et al., 2025). We compare against representative diffusion caching methods, including TeaCache (Liu et al., 2025a), TaylorSeer (Liu et al., 2025b), MagCache (Ma et al., 2026), DiCache (Bu et al., 2025), HiCache (Feng et al., 2026), SeaCache (Chung et al., 2026), and SenCache (Haghighi and Alahi, 2026). We enable classifier-free guidance (CFG) (Ho and Salimans, 2022) for Qwen-Image-2512 and Wan 2.1, using identical guidance settings for full inference and all accelerated methods.

Evaluation Metrics. We evaluate 200 DrawBench prompts (Saharia et al., 2022) with three random seeds for text-to-image generation and 944 VBench prompts (Huang et al., 2024) with five random seeds for text-to-video generation. Following prior work (Bu et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025a), we report latency, speedup, FLOPs, and peak allocated GPU memory. ImageReward and CLIP Score assess image quality, while VBench evaluates video quality. LPIPS (Zhang et al., 2018), SSIM (Wang et al., 2004), and PSNR measure reconstruction fidelity against full inference. All results are averaged over random seeds.

Implementation Details. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU. We use 10 offline calibration trajectories to estimate the cross-timestep covariance statistics. Detailed model configurations, profiling protocols, and baseline hyperparameters are provided in Appendix B.

4.2 Main Results

Text-to-image generation.

Table 1 compares PoSTCache with representative caching methods and direct step-reduction baselines on FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image-2512. Across both models and acceleration regimes, PoSTCache consistently improves reconstruction fidelity at comparable or higher speedups while largely preserving semantic quality, yielding the strongest efficiency–fidelity trade-off overall. As illustrated in Figure 4, these quantitative gains are accompanied by better preservation of object identity, geometric structure, and fine-grained appearance than competing caching methods. Qualitative comparison on Qwen-Image-2512 is provided in Appendix C.8.

Text-to-video generation.

Table 2 reports the results on Wan 2.1, CogVideoX, and OpenSora 1.2. PoSTCache likewise achieves consistently stronger reconstruction fidelity under comparable computation budgets while maintaining competitive overall VBench quality. Its advantage persists across both moderate and aggressive acceleration settings, as well as across different architectures and resolutions, demonstrating the effectiveness of PoSTCache in limiting accumulated spatiotemporal trajectory errors. Additional qualitative comparisons are provided in Appendix C.8.

4.3 Ablation Studies

Component Analysis.

Table 3(a) evaluates the contributions of postdictive smoothing and anchor selection under the same computation budget. Postdictive smoothing consistently improves all three selection strategies, confirming that anchor innovations provide effective corrective information for skipped predictions. The PVR selector also outperforms fixed intervals and the MagCache selector, and combining PVR selection with postdictive smoothing yields the best performance.

Generality across Forward Caching Strategies.

Table 3(b) evaluates PoSTCache with MagCache and DiCache as forward caching strategies. Postdictive smoothing improves reconstruction fidelity with only marginal runtime overhead, while combining it with PVR selection provides substantial additional gains. These results demonstrate that PoSTCache is compatible with different forward proposal mechanisms.

Additional Analysis.

Appendices C.2–C.7 further examine calibration-size robustness, validate the PVR objective and schedule transferability, compare alternative global scheduling objectives, and analyze temporal weighting, dense-prefix anchors, and anchor-state consistency. These results support our default design choices, quantify the modest one-time offline calibration cost, and confirm negligible online overhead and favorable quality–efficiency trade-offs.

5 Conclusion and Future Work

In this work, we presented PoSTCache, a training-free and plug-and-play framework that reformulates diffusion caching as a revisable trajectory inference problem. By using feedback from subsequent full-computation steps, PoSTCache retrospectively refines skipped predictions and reintegrates the corrected sampling trajectory. Viewing anchors as sources of corrective feedback, we further introduced a posterior variance reduction criterion to select informative anchors according to their expected reduction in surrogate trajectory uncertainty. Extensive experiments on representative image and video generation models demonstrate that PoSTCache consistently improves the efficiency–fidelity trade-off and can be readily integrated with different forward caching strategies. Currently, PoSTCache estimates a shared anchor configuration from offline trajectories and applies it uniformly to all samples. Although this design is simple and effective, it may not fully capture sample-specific trajectory dynamics. A promising direction for future work is to combine the offline uncertainty structure with lightweight online observations, enabling the anchor schedule to adapt to each sampling trajectory without introducing substantial inference overhead.
