Appendix A Theoretical Background and Derivations

A.1 Sequential Trajectory Estimation View of Diffusion and Flow Sampling

A broad class of diffusion, flow-matching, and rectified-flow samplers can be expressed as a sequence of model predictions and numerical state updates:

uk=fθ​(xk,τk),xk+1=𝒮k​(xk,uk,τk),u_{k}=f_{\theta}(x_{k},\tau_{k}),\qquad x_{k+1}=\mathcal{S}_{k}(x_{k},u_{k},\tau_{k}), (15)

where xkx_{k} is the latent state at the kk-th sampling step, τk\tau_{k} is the corresponding noise or time level, uku_{k} is the model prediction consumed by the sampler, and 𝒮k\mathcal{S}_{k} denotes the scheduler or numerical solver. Depending on the model parameterization, uku_{k} may represent noise, a clean sample estimate, a velocity, or a flow vector.

Equation (15) defines a recursive trajectory estimation process. At each step, the model predicts the local direction of the trajectory from the current latent state, and the solver propagates this prediction to the next state. This structure resembles sequential Bayesian estimation, in which an estimate is repeatedly updated using the information available at the current step.

Under cache-based acceleration, some full model predictions are replaced by forward approximations. Let

u~k=uk−ek\widetilde{u}_{k}=u_{k}-e_{k} (16)

denote the cached prediction, where eke_{k} is the corresponding approximation error. The approximate sampling trajectory then evolves according to

x~k+1=𝒮k​(x~k,u~k,τk).\widetilde{x}_{k+1}=\mathcal{S}_{k}\left(\widetilde{x}_{k},\widetilde{u}_{k},\tau_{k}\right). (17)

Because each state is used as the input to subsequent model evaluations and solver updates, an error introduced at one step can affect all later states.

To make this propagation explicit, define the latent-state deviation δ​xk=x~k−xk\delta x_{k}=\widetilde{x}_{k}-x_{k}. A first-order expansion of the solver around the full-computation trajectory gives

δ​xk+1≈Ak​δ​xk−Bk​ek,Ak=∂𝒮k∂xk,Bk=∂𝒮k∂uk.\delta x_{k+1}\approx A_{k}\delta x_{k}-B_{k}e_{k},\qquad A_{k}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{S}_{k}}{\partial x_{k}},\qquad B_{k}=\frac{\partial\mathcal{S}_{k}}{\partial u_{k}}. (18)

Thus, the deviation at step k+1k+1 depends not only on the current prediction error but also on the deviation accumulated from previous steps. Repeatedly applying Eq. (18) over a skipped interval a<k<ba<k<b yields

δxb≈Ab−1⋯Aaδxa−∑j=ab−1(Ab−1⋯Aj+1)Bjej,\delta x_{b}\approx A_{b-1}\cdots A_{a}\delta x_{a}-\sum_{j=a}^{b-1}\left(A_{b-1}\cdots A_{j+1}\right)B_{j}e_{j}, (19)

where an empty matrix product is understood as the identity. Consequently, even individually small approximation errors may accumulate and alter the subsequent sampling trajectory.

Suppose that step bb is selected as a full-computation anchor. A complete model evaluation at the current latent state produces u¯b=fθ​(x~b,τb)\bar{u}_{b}=f_{\theta}(\widetilde{x}_{b},\tau_{b}), while the forward caching rule also provides a proposal u~b\widetilde{u}_{b}. Their discrepancy,

rb=u¯b−u~b,r_{b}=\bar{u}_{b}-\widetilde{u}_{b}, (20)

is the anchor innovation. Although rbr_{b} does not directly observe each preceding error eke_{k}, it reveals the discrepancy between the forward approximation and the newly available full computation. Since the preceding cache errors jointly influence the latent state and the forward proposal at step bb, the innovation can contain information about the errors accumulated over the skipped interval.

More formally, let the centered intermediate error eke_{k} and future innovation rbr_{b} be locally approximated by a joint Gaussian distribution. Conditioning on the observed innovation gives

𝔼⁡[ek∣rb]=Σek​rb​(Σrb​rb+Rb)−1​rb,\mathbb{E}\left[e_{k}\mid r_{b}\right]=\Sigma_{e_{k}r_{b}}\left(\Sigma_{r_{b}r_{b}}+R_{b}\right)^{-1}r_{b}, (21)

where Σek​rb\Sigma_{e_{k}r_{b}} is the cross-covariance between the intermediate proposal error and the future innovation, and RbR_{b} accounts for residual uncertainty in the future evidence. The corresponding corrected prediction therefore has the generic form

u^k=u~k+Gk←b​rb,Gk←b=Σek​rb​(Σrb​rb+Rb)−1.\widehat{u}_{k}=\widetilde{u}_{k}+G_{k\leftarrow b}r_{b},\qquad G_{k\leftarrow b}=\Sigma_{e_{k}r_{b}}\left(\Sigma_{r_{b}r_{b}}+R_{b}\right)^{-1}. (22)

That is, a forward estimate is revised by propagating a future innovation backward through a covariance-dependent smoothing gain. This conditional estimation view motivates the postdictive correction used by PoSTCache. The standard linear Gaussian filtering and smoothing identities underlying Eq. (22) are reviewed in Appendix A.2.

A.2 Linear Gaussian Filtering and Smoothing

Consider a linear Gaussian state-space model

zt+1=At​zt+wt,yt=Ht​zt+vt,z_{t+1}=A_{t}z_{t}+w_{t},\qquad y_{t}=H_{t}z_{t}+v_{t}, (23)

where wt∼𝒩⁡(0,Qt)w_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,Q_{t}) and vt∼𝒩⁡(0,Rt)v_{t}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,R_{t}).

Given the filtering distribution

p(zt∣y1:t)=𝒩(mt|t,Pt|t),p(z_{t}\mid y_{1:t})=\mathcal{N}(m_{t\mid t},P_{t\mid t}), (24)

the one-step predictive distribution is

p(zt+1∣y1:t)=𝒩(mt+1|t,Pt+1|t),p(z_{t+1}\mid y_{1:t})=\mathcal{N}(m_{t+1\mid t},P_{t+1\mid t}), (25)

where

mt+1|t\displaystyle m_{t+1\mid t} =At​mt|t,\displaystyle=A_{t}m_{t\mid t}, (26)
Pt+1|t\displaystyle P_{t+1\mid t} =At​Pt|t​At⊤+Qt.\displaystyle=A_{t}P_{t\mid t}A_{t}^{\top}+Q_{t}. (27)

The Rauch–Tung–Striebel smoother (Rauch et al., 1965) performs a backward recursion after the forward filtering pass:

mt|T\displaystyle m_{t\mid T} =mt|t+Gt​(mt+1|T−mt+1|t),\displaystyle=m_{t\mid t}+G_{t}\left(m_{t+1\mid T}-m_{t+1\mid t}\right), (28)
Pt|T\displaystyle P_{t\mid T} =Pt|t+Gt​(Pt+1|T−Pt+1|t)​Gt⊤,\displaystyle=P_{t\mid t}+G_{t}\left(P_{t+1\mid T}-P_{t+1\mid t}\right)G_{t}^{\top}, (29)

with smoothing gain

Gt=Pt|t​At⊤​Pt+1|t−1.G_{t}=P_{t\mid t}A_{t}^{\top}P_{t+1\mid t}^{-1}. (30)

The innovation mt+1|T−mt+1|tm_{t+1\mid T}-m_{t+1\mid t} measures the discrepancy between the future smoothed estimate and its forward prediction, which is propagated backward to revise the current estimate.

More generally, suppose an intermediate state ztz_{t} and future evidence yby_{b} follow a joint Gaussian distribution:

[ztyb]∼𝒩⁡([mtmb],[Pt​tPt​bPb​tPb​b+Rb]).\begin{bmatrix}z_{t}\\ y_{b}\end{bmatrix}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(\begin{bmatrix}m_{t}\\ m_{b}\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}P_{tt}&P_{tb}\\ P_{bt}&P_{bb}+R_{b}\end{bmatrix}\right). (31)

Applying the Gaussian conditioning identity gives

p⁡(zt∣yb)=𝒩⁡(mt|b,Pt|b),p(z_{t}\mid y_{b})=\mathcal{N}\left(m_{t\mid b},P_{t\mid b}\right), (32)

where

mt|b\displaystyle m_{t\mid b} =mt+Pt​b​(Pb​b+Rb)−1​(yb−mb),\displaystyle=m_{t}+P_{tb}(P_{bb}+R_{b})^{-1}(y_{b}-m_{b}), (33)
Pt|b\displaystyle P_{t\mid b} =Pt​t−Pt​b​(Pb​b+Rb)−1​Pb​t.\displaystyle=P_{tt}-P_{tb}(P_{bb}+R_{b})^{-1}P_{bt}. (34)

The conditional mean has the generic form

smoothed estimate=forward estimate+smoothing gain×future innovation.\text{smoothed estimate}=\text{forward estimate}+\text{smoothing gain}\times\text{future innovation}. (35)

Meanwhile, the posterior covariance subtracts a positive-semidefinite term from the prior covariance. Therefore, informative future evidence both corrects the forward estimate and reduces its remaining uncertainty. This linear Gaussian result motivates the postdictive correction and posterior variance reduction formulations used in our method.

A.3 Derivation of Postdictive Smoothing

Consider a cache interval bounded by two consecutive full-computation anchors a<ba<b. For an intermediate step kk, define the proposal error as

ek=u¯k−u~k,a<k<b,e_{k}=\bar{u}_{k}-\widetilde{u}_{k},\qquad a<k<b, (36)

where u¯k\bar{u}_{k} denotes the hypothetical full-computation prediction evaluated at the same forward state.

We locally approximate the temporal evolution of the proposal errors by a first-order stochastic system:

ej+1=Fj​ej+ξj,ξj∼𝒩⁡(0,Qj),e_{j+1}=F_{j}e_{j}+\xi_{j},\qquad\xi_{j}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,Q_{j}), (37)

where FjF_{j} is the Jacobian of the local error transition around the forward trajectory. Propagating this system from step kk to anchor bb gives

eb=Φb←kek+ξk:b,Φb←k=Fb−1⋯Fk,e_{b}=\Phi_{b\leftarrow k}e_{k}+\xi_{k:b},\qquad\Phi_{b\leftarrow k}=F_{b-1}\cdots F_{k}, (38)

where ξk:b\xi_{k:b} aggregates the process noise over the interval.

Assume that the intermediate proposal error follows a Gaussian prior

ek∼𝒩⁡(0,Ck​k).e_{k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,C_{kk}). (39)

At the future full-computation anchor, the innovation

rb=u¯b−u~b=ebr_{b}=\bar{u}_{b}-\widetilde{u}_{b}=e_{b} (40)

directly reveals the terminal proposal error.

Equation (38) induces the joint Gaussian distribution

[ekrb]∼𝒩⁡(0,[Ck​kCk​bCb​kCb​b]),\begin{bmatrix}e_{k}\\ r_{b}\end{bmatrix}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\begin{bmatrix}C_{kk}&C_{kb}\\ C_{bk}&C_{bb}\end{bmatrix}\right), (41)

where

Ck​b\displaystyle C_{kb} =Ck​k​Φb←k⊤,\displaystyle=C_{kk}\Phi_{b\leftarrow k}^{\top}, (42)
Cb​b\displaystyle C_{bb} =Φb←kCk​kΦb←k⊤+Qk:b,\displaystyle=\Phi_{b\leftarrow k}C_{kk}\Phi_{b\leftarrow k}^{\top}+Q_{k:b}, (43)

and Qk:bQ_{k:b} denotes the covariance of the accumulated process noise.

Applying the Gaussian conditioning identity to Eq. (41) yields

p⁡(ek∣rb)=𝒩⁡(Gk←b​rb,Ck​k|b),p(e_{k}\mid r_{b})=\mathcal{N}\left(G_{k\leftarrow b}r_{b},C_{kk\mid b}\right), (44)

with smoothing gain

Gk←b=Ck​b​Cb​b−1,G_{k\leftarrow b}=C_{kb}C_{bb}^{-1}, (45)

and posterior covariance

Ck​k|b=Ck​k−Ck​b​Cb​b−1​Cb​k.C_{kk\mid b}=C_{kk}-C_{kb}C_{bb}^{-1}C_{bk}. (46)

The conditional mean is the minimum-mean-square-error estimate of eke_{k}:

e^k=𝔼⁡[ek∣rb]=Gk←b​rb.\widehat{e}_{k}=\mathbb{E}[e_{k}\mid r_{b}]=G_{k\leftarrow b}r_{b}. (47)

Since u¯k=u~k+ek\bar{u}_{k}=\widetilde{u}_{k}+e_{k}, the corresponding estimate of the full-computation prediction is

u^k=u~k+Gk←b​(u¯b−u~b).\widehat{u}_{k}=\widetilde{u}_{k}+G_{k\leftarrow b}\left(\bar{u}_{b}-\widetilde{u}_{b}\right). (48)

The covariance reduction induced by the future anchor is

Ck​k−Ck​k|b=Ck​b​Cb​b−1​Cb​k⪰0.C_{kk}-C_{kk\mid b}=C_{kb}C_{bb}^{-1}C_{bk}\succeq 0. (49)

Thus, under the assumed linear Gaussian model, conditioning on an informative future anchor cannot increase the uncertainty of the intermediate proposal error.

Direct estimation of the full matrix gain in Eq. (45) is impractical for high-dimensional model predictions. We therefore use the isotropic approximation

Gk←b≈wk|a,b​I.G_{k\leftarrow b}\approx w_{k\mid a,b}I. (50)

Motivated by the empirical observation in Sec. 3.2 that the alignment between intermediate errors and the anchor innovation increases toward the future anchor, we set

wk|a,b=ηk−ηaηb−ηa.w_{k\mid a,b}=\frac{\eta_{k}-\eta_{a}}{\eta_{b}-\eta_{a}}. (51)

This yields the lightweight postdictive correction used in the main text:

u^k=u~k+wk|a,b​(u¯b−u~b).\widehat{u}_{k}=\widetilde{u}_{k}+w_{k\mid a,b}\left(\bar{u}_{b}-\widetilde{u}_{b}\right). (52)

A.4 Derivation of Posterior Variance Reduction Selection

Cross-timestep uncertainty model.

For each offline sample nn, we store the complete sequence of full-computation model predictions

zk(n)=u¯k(n)∈ℝD,k=1,…,T,z_{k}^{(n)}=\bar{u}_{k}^{(n)}\in\mathbb{R}^{D},\qquad k=1,\ldots,T, (53)

where u¯k(n)\bar{u}_{k}^{(n)} is the prediction consumed by the numerical solver after applying the same guidance and output-parameterization transformations as in inference. All non-temporal dimensions are flattened without projection. We define the empirical mean and block covariance as

μk\displaystyle\mu_{k} =1N​∑n=1Nzk(n),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}z_{k}^{(n)}, (54)
Σi​j\displaystyle\Sigma_{ij} =1N​∑n=1N(zi(n)−μi)​(zj(n)−μj)⊤.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left(z_{i}^{(n)}-\mu_{i}\right)\left(z_{j}^{(n)}-\mu_{j}\right)^{\top}. (55)

Explicitly storing every block Σi​j∈ℝD×D\Sigma_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times D} is prohibitively expensive. We therefore summarize each block by its normalized trace:

Ki​j\displaystyle K_{ij} =1D​tr⁡(Σi​j)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{D}\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{ij}) (56)
=1N​D​∑n=1N⟨zi(n)−μi,zj(n)−μj⟩.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{ND}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\left\langle z_{i}^{(n)}-\mu_{i},\,z_{j}^{(n)}-\mu_{j}\right\rangle. (57)

Thus, K∈ℝT×TK\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times T} provides a lightweight timestep-level summary of the covariance structure of the complete trajectories. The resulting empirical kernel is positive semidefinite. In implementation, we add a small fixed diagonal jitter before matrix solving for numerical stability and use KK to denote the stabilized kernel below.

Let δ​zk=zk−μk\delta z_{k}=z_{k}-\mu_{k}. We adopt the isotropic covariance surrogate

δz1:T∼𝒩(0,K⊗ID).\delta z_{1:T}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\,K\otimes I_{D}\right). (58)

For an anchor set AA, the corresponding centered trajectory states are observed as

yA=δ​zA.y_{A}=\delta z_{A}. (59)
Posterior mean and variance.

The joint Gaussian distribution of the centered state at timestep tt and the observed anchor states is

[δ​ztyA]∼𝒩⁡(0,[Kt​t​IDKt​A⊗IDKA​t⊗IDKA​A⊗ID]).\begin{bmatrix}\delta z_{t}\\ y_{A}\end{bmatrix}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\,\begin{bmatrix}K_{tt}I_{D}&K_{tA}\otimes I_{D}\\ K_{At}\otimes I_{D}&K_{AA}\otimes I_{D}\end{bmatrix}\right). (60)

Gaussian conditioning gives

p⁡(δ​zt∣yA)=𝒩⁡(δ​z^tA,Vt​(A)​ID),p(\delta z_{t}\mid y_{A})=\mathcal{N}\left(\widehat{\delta z}_{t}^{A},\,V_{t}(A)I_{D}\right), (61)

where

δ​z^tA\displaystyle\widehat{\delta z}_{t}^{A} =[Kt​A​KA​A−1⊗ID]​yA,\displaystyle=\left[K_{tA}K_{AA}^{-1}\otimes I_{D}\right]y_{A}, (62)
Vt​(A)\displaystyle V_{t}(A) =Kt​t−Kt​A​KA​A−1​KA​t.\displaystyle=K_{tt}-K_{tA}K_{AA}^{-1}K_{At}. (63)

For a single anchor A={b}A=\{b\}, the posterior mean reduces to

δ​z^t{b}=Kt​bKb​b​yb.\widehat{\delta z}_{t}^{\{b\}}=\frac{K_{tb}}{K_{bb}}y_{b}. (64)

The posterior variance measures the trajectory uncertainty remaining after conditioning on the selected anchors. Under the isotropic surrogate, the corresponding conditional mean-squared error is

𝔼⁡[‖δ​zt−δ​z^tA‖22|yA]=D​Vt​(A).\mathbb{E}\left[\left\|\delta z_{t}-\widehat{\delta z}_{t}^{A}\right\|_{2}^{2}\,\middle|\,y_{A}\right]=D\,V_{t}(A). (65)
Connection to postdictive correction.

Consider a candidate anchor s∉As\notin A. We define the residual error at timestep tt and the innovation introduced by candidate ss as

ϵtA=δ​zt−δ​z^tA,νsA=ys−δ​z^sA.\epsilon_{t}^{A}=\delta z_{t}-\widehat{\delta z}_{t}^{A},\qquad\nu_{s}^{A}=y_{s}-\widehat{\delta z}_{s}^{A}. (66)

Conditioned on the current anchor observations yAy_{A}, these quantities follow the joint Gaussian distribution

([ϵtAνsA]∣yA)∼𝒩⁡(0,[Vt​(A)Ct​s|ACt​s|AVs​(A)]⊗ID),(\begin{bmatrix}\epsilon_{t}^{A}\\ \nu_{s}^{A}\end{bmatrix}\,\mid\,y_{A})\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\,\begin{bmatrix}V_{t}(A)&C_{ts\mid A}\\ C_{ts\mid A}&V_{s}(A)\end{bmatrix}\otimes I_{D}\right), (67)

where

Ct​s|A=Kt​s−Kt​A​KA​A−1​KA​s.C_{ts\mid A}=K_{ts}-K_{tA}K_{AA}^{-1}K_{As}. (68)

Therefore, Ct​s|A​IDC_{ts\mid A}I_{D} is precisely the conditional covariance between the residual error at timestep tt and the innovation of candidate anchor ss under the trajectory surrogate.

Conditioning additionally on νsA\nu_{s}^{A} gives the posterior-mean update

δ​z^tA∪{s}=δ​z^tA+Ct​s|AVs​(A)​νsA.\widehat{\delta z}_{t}^{A\cup\{s\}}=\widehat{\delta z}_{t}^{A}+\frac{C_{ts\mid A}}{V_{s}(A)}\nu_{s}^{A}. (69)

This update has the same form as the linear Gaussian postdictive correction in Eq. (7), with Ct​s|A/Vs​(A)C_{ts\mid A}/V_{s}(A) acting as an isotropic smoothing gain.

The corresponding posterior variance satisfies the rank-one update

Vt​(A∪{s})=Vt​(A)−Ct​s|A 2Vs​(A).V_{t}(A\cup\{s\})=V_{t}(A)-\frac{C_{ts\mid A}^{\,2}}{V_{s}(A)}. (70)

Consequently, observing candidate anchor ss reduces the conditional mean-squared residual error at timestep tt by

D⁡[Vt​(A)−Vt​(A∪{s})]=D​Ct​s|A 2Vs​(A).D\left[V_{t}(A)-V_{t}(A\cup\{s\})\right]=D\frac{C_{ts\mid A}^{\,2}}{V_{s}(A)}. (71)

Thus, Ct​s|A 2/Vs​(A)C_{ts\mid A}^{\,2}/V_{s}(A) directly measures the expected residual variance reduction provided by candidate anchor ss.

The conditional mean above is a statistical surrogate induced by the complete-trajectory covariance and need not coincide with the specific forward proposal used by a practical caching method. Accordingly, the resulting criterion should be interpreted as a proposal-agnostic measure of intrinsic anchor informativeness.

Budgeted anchor selection.

Given a full-computation budget ℬ\mathcal{B}, we minimize the weighted uncertainty of the complete trajectory:

A⋆=arg⁡min⁡∑t=1TA0⊆A|A|≤ℬ⁡γt​Vt​(A),A^{\star}=\arg\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}A_{0}\subseteq A\\ |A|\leq\mathcal{B}\end{subarray}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma_{t}V_{t}(A), (72)

where A0A_{0} contains the dense-prefix anchors and the final denoising step, and γt\gamma_{t} is a scheduler-aware temporal weight.

By Eq. (70), the marginal reduction in weighted trajectory uncertainty obtained by adding candidate ss is

Δ⁡(s∣A)=∑t=1Tγt​Ct​s|A 2Vs​(A).\Delta(s\mid A)=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma_{t}\frac{C_{ts\mid A}^{\,2}}{V_{s}(A)}. (73)

The common factor DD in the corresponding mean-squared error reduction does not affect candidate ranking and is therefore omitted. At each iteration, we select

s⋆=arg⁡maxs∉A⁡Δ⁡(s∣A),s^{\star}=\arg\max_{s\notin A}\Delta(s\mid A), (74)

update the posterior covariance, and repeat until the computation budget is exhausted.

Appendix B Experimental Settings

B.1 Models, Datasets, and Generation Configurations

We evaluate PoSTCache on five representative image and video generation models. For text-to-image generation, we use FLUX.1-dev (Labs, 2024) and Qwen-Image-2512 (Wu et al., 2025), evaluated on DrawBench (Saharia et al., 2022). For text-to-video generation, we use Wan 2.1 (Wan et al., 2025), CogVideoX (Yang et al., 2025), and OpenSora 1.2 (Zheng et al., 2024), evaluated on VBench (Huang et al., 2024) prompts.

Table 4 summarizes the generation configuration of each model. CogVideoX is evaluated in FP16 following its officially recommended inference configuration, while the other models use BF16. Unless otherwise specified, all remaining parameters follow the default configurations of the corresponding official implementations.

B.2 PoSTCache Configuration

PoSTCache consists of a forward proposal strategy, postdictive smoothing and reintegration, and posterior variance reduction anchor selection. Unless otherwise specified, the latest full-computation prediction is reused as the forward proposal. Within each cache interval [a,b][a,b], the postdictive gain is set to the relative sampling progress wk|a,b=(ηk−ηa)/(ηb−ηa)w_{k\mid a,b}=(\eta_{k}-\eta_{a})/(\eta_{b}-\eta_{a}).

For offline anchor selection, we collect N=10N=10 complete denoising trajectories for each model. All non-temporal dimensions are flattened without projection when constructing the cross-timestep covariance kernel. The empirical kernel is normalized by both the number of calibration samples and the trajectory dimension.

Scheduler-aware temporal weighting.

Many diffusion schedulers use non-uniform discretizations with relatively small solver intervals in the early denoising stage and progressively larger intervals later. Such dense sampling reflects the need to track the trajectory at a finer temporal resolution. We therefore use the local solver spacing as a scheduler-aware proxy for timestep importance, assigning larger weights to more densely sampled regions rather than treating all denoising steps uniformly. Let δk\delta_{k} denote the local scheduler spacing at timestep kk. When the sampler exposes a noise-level sequence {σk}k=0T\{\sigma_{k}\}_{k=0}^{T}, we use the exact transition spacing

δk=|σk+1−σk|,k=0,…,T−1.\delta_{k}=\left|\sigma_{k+1}-\sigma_{k}\right|,\qquad k=0,\ldots,T-1. (75)

Otherwise, given scheduler timesteps {τk}k=1T\{\tau_{k}\}_{k=1}^{T}, we approximate the local spacing by

δk={|τ2−τ1|,k=1,12​(|τk−τk−1|+|τk+1−τk|),1<k<T,|τT−τT−1|,k=T.\delta_{k}=\begin{cases}|\tau_{2}-\tau_{1}|,&k=1,\\[2.0pt] \frac{1}{2}\left(|\tau_{k}-\tau_{k-1}|+|\tau_{k+1}-\tau_{k}|\right),&1<k<T,\\[2.0pt] |\tau_{T}-\tau_{T-1}|,&k=T.\end{cases} (76)

The unnormalized temporal weight is

γ~k=(medianj⁡δjδk+ϵ)p,\widetilde{\gamma}_{k}=\left(\frac{\operatorname{median}_{j}\delta_{j}}{\delta_{k}+\epsilon}\right)^{p}, (77)

where pp controls the weighting strength. We first normalize the weights to unit mean, clip their range, and renormalize:

γ¯k=γ~k1T​∑j=1Tγ~j,γk=clip⁡(γ¯k,γmin,γmax)1T​∑j=1Tclip⁡(γ¯j,γmin,γmax).\bar{\gamma}_{k}=\frac{\widetilde{\gamma}_{k}}{\frac{1}{T}\sum_{j=1}^{T}\widetilde{\gamma}_{j}},\qquad\gamma_{k}=\frac{\operatorname{clip}\left(\bar{\gamma}_{k},\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}\right)}{\frac{1}{T}\sum_{j=1}^{T}\operatorname{clip}\left(\bar{\gamma}_{j},\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max}\right)}. (78)

Unless otherwise specified, we use p=0.5p=0.5 and (γmin,γmax)=(0.5,2.0)(\gamma_{\min},\gamma_{\max})=(0.5,2.0).

Detailed model-specific settings are reported in Table 5.

For all models and variants, we use N=10N=10 calibration trajectories and the same scheduler-aware temporal weighting. The final denoising step is always included as a mandatory anchor. The Fast and Slow variants differ only in the full-computation budget ℬ\mathcal{B} and dense-prefix length.

B.3 Baseline Generation Settings

We compare PoSTCache with representative training-free diffusion caching methods, including TeaCache (Liu et al., 2025a), TaylorSeer (Liu et al., 2025b), MagCache (Ma et al., 2026), DiCache (Bu et al., 2025), HiCache (Feng et al., 2026), SeaCache (Chung et al., 2026), and SenCache (Haghighi and Alahi, 2026). We use the official implementations whenever available. For each baseline, we perform a lightweight runtime calibration on a small profiling set (typically two prompts), varying only its acceleration-control parameters to identify configurations with latency closest to the corresponding Fast and Slow regimes of PoSTCache. This calibration uses latency only and does not access any generation-quality metric. The selected configurations are then fixed and evaluated on the complete benchmark using the same prompt–seed pairs as the other methods. Tables 6 and 7 report the complete configurations.

B.4 Evaluation and Implementation Details

Hardware and software.

All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA H200 GPU in a Linux environment with Python 3.12.13, CUDA Toolkit 13.0.2, PyTorch 2.11.0, Diffusers 0.37.1, and Transformers 5.4.0. The complete environment configuration and dependency list will be released with the code repository.

Random seeds.

We evaluate DrawBench and VBench using three and five different base seeds, respectively, with one sample generated per prompt in each run. Specifically, the image experiments use base seeds {0,2026,2027}\{0,2026,2027\}, while the video experiments use base seeds {100,200,300,400,500}\{100,200,300,400,500\}. For a prompt with global index pp, its seed is deterministically assigned as

sp=sbase+p.s_{p}=s_{\mathrm{base}}+p. (79)

Full inference and all accelerated methods use identical prompt–seed pairs, independent of batch size or data-parallel partitioning. Results are averaged over the corresponding base-seed runs.

Latency measurement.

Inference latency is measured during the actual generation of the DrawBench and VBench evaluation samples rather than using isolated synthetic inputs. For each prompt–seed pair, wall-clock time is recorded using time.perf_counter() with CUDA synchronization before each timestamp to ensure that asynchronous GPU operations are completed. The reported latency is the arithmetic mean over all evaluated prompts and random seeds for each model and method under the same hardware and software environment. Output serialization and metric computation are excluded from the timing.

The speedup ratio is computed as

Speedup=LatencyfullLatencymethod.\mathrm{Speedup}=\frac{\mathrm{Latency}_{\mathrm{full}}}{\mathrm{Latency}_{\mathrm{method}}}. (80)
FLOPs and memory.

FLOPs and GPU memory are profiled over the generation loop. FLOPs are estimated using torch.profiler with FLOP counting enabled, and the estimates reported by all supported ATen operators are summed. The profiler primarily provides FLOP metadata for matrix multiplication and convolution; therefore, the reported FLOPs do not necessarily include every element-wise or framework-level operation. Before each profiled generation, we synchronize the GPU and reset the CUDA peak-memory statistics. Peak memory is reported as the maximum allocated CUDA memory obtained from torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated(), expressed in GiB. We report allocated rather than reserved memory to reflect the peak memory actively used by tensors during inference.

Offline profiling cost.

Offline trajectory collection and anchor selection are performed once for each model. Their costs are excluded from per-sample inference latency because the resulting anchor schedule is shared across all evaluation samples.

B.5 Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate both inference efficiency and generation quality. Efficiency is measured by latency, speedup, FLOPs, and peak GPU memory. Generation quality is evaluated using semantic-quality metrics and paired reconstruction metrics.

ImageReward.

ImageReward (Xu et al., 2023) is a learned human-preference metric for text-to-image generation. It evaluates the consistency and perceptual quality of a generated image with respect to its text prompt. A higher score indicates stronger alignment with human preference.

CLIP Score.

CLIP Score (Hessel et al., 2021) measures text–image alignment using the cosine similarity between pretrained CLIP text and image embeddings. We use the CLIP-ViT-Base-Patch32 model for feature extraction. Higher values indicate stronger semantic consistency with the input prompt.

VBench.

VBench (Huang et al., 2024) evaluates video generation along multiple spatial, temporal, semantic, and perceptual dimensions. We use the official evaluation implementation and report its aggregated overall score. Higher scores indicate better video quality.

LPIPS.

Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) (Zhang et al., 2018) measures perceptual discrepancy using deep visual features. Let x^\hat{x} and x⋆x^{\star} denote the accelerated and full-inference outputs, respectively. LPIPS is computed as

LPIPS⁡(x^,x⋆)=∑l1Hl​Wl​∑h,w‖𝐰l⊙(ϕ~l​(x^)h,w−ϕ~l​(x⋆)h,w)‖22,\operatorname{LPIPS}(\hat{x},x^{\star})=\sum_{l}\frac{1}{H_{l}W_{l}}\sum_{h,w}\left\|\mathbf{w}_{l}\odot\left(\widetilde{\phi}_{l}(\hat{x})_{h,w}-\widetilde{\phi}_{l}(x^{\star})_{h,w}\right)\right\|_{2}^{2}, (81)

where ϕ~l​(⋅)\widetilde{\phi}_{l}(\cdot) denotes the channel-normalized feature at layer ll, and 𝐰l\mathbf{w}_{l} contains the learned channel-wise weights. We use AlexNet as the feature-extraction backbone. Lower values indicate that the accelerated output is perceptually closer to the corresponding full-inference output.

SSIM.

Structural Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) (Wang et al., 2004) compares the luminance, contrast, and structural information of the accelerated and full-inference outputs. For two local image windows x^\hat{x} and x⋆x^{\star}, it is defined as

SSIM⁡(x^,x⋆)=(2​μx^​μx⋆+C1)​(2​σx^​x⋆+C2)(μx^2+μx⋆2+C1)​(σx^2+σx⋆2+C2),\operatorname{SSIM}(\hat{x},x^{\star})=\frac{(2\mu_{\hat{x}}\mu_{x^{\star}}+C_{1})(2\sigma_{\hat{x}x^{\star}}+C_{2})}{(\mu_{\hat{x}}^{2}+\mu_{x^{\star}}^{2}+C_{1})(\sigma_{\hat{x}}^{2}+\sigma_{x^{\star}}^{2}+C_{2})}, (82)

where μx^\mu_{\hat{x}} and μx⋆\mu_{x^{\star}} are the local means, σx^2\sigma_{\hat{x}}^{2} and σx⋆2\sigma_{x^{\star}}^{2} are the local variances, σx^​x⋆\sigma_{\hat{x}x^{\star}} is their covariance, and C1C_{1} and C2C_{2} are stabilizing constants. The final score is averaged over all spatial windows. Higher values indicate stronger structural similarity.

PSNR.

Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio measures pixel-level reconstruction fidelity:

PSNR=10​log10​(R2MSE),\mathrm{PSNR}=10\log_{10}\left(\frac{R^{2}}{\mathrm{MSE}}\right), (83)

where RR is the maximum representable pixel value. Higher PSNR indicates smaller pixel-level reconstruction error.

For video reconstruction, LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR are computed between temporally corresponding frames and then averaged over frames and evaluation prompts.

Appendix C Additional Experimental Results and Analysis

C.1 Additional Trajectory Analysis

Additional trajectory visualization.

To complement the quantitative trajectory analysis in Sec. 3.2, we visualize the denoising trajectories of full inference, forward-only caching, and PoSTCache in a low-dimensional space. As shown in Figure 5, forward-only caching progressively deviates from the full-inference trajectory, whereas postdictive smoothing consistently pulls the trajectory toward the full-inference reference after future anchors become available. This behavior is observed across both image and video generation models.

Evaluation details for Figure 2(c).

For a candidate future anchor ss following the most recent full-computation anchor aa, we quantify its local cache risk under nearest reuse as

Rlocal​(s∣a)=1N​D​∑n=1N∑k=a+1sγk​‖u¯k(n)−u¯a(n)‖22R_{\mathrm{local}}(s\mid a)=\frac{1}{ND}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{k=a+1}^{s}\gamma_{k}\left\|\bar{u}_{k}^{(n)}-\bar{u}_{a}^{(n)}\right\|_{2}^{2} (84)

To measure its trajectory-level corrective value, we use the same relative-position gain as PoSTCache, wk|a,s=(ηk−ηa)/(ηs−ηa)w_{k\mid a,s}=(\eta_{k}-\eta_{a})/(\eta_{s}-\eta_{a}), and define

Gfixed​(s∣a)=1N​D​∑n=1N∑k=a+1s−1γk​[‖ek(n,a)‖22−‖ek(n,a)−wk|a,s​rs(n,a)‖22]G_{\mathrm{fixed}}(s\mid a)=\frac{1}{ND}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{k=a+1}^{s-1}\gamma_{k}\left[\|e_{k}^{(n,a)}\|_{2}^{2}-\|e_{k}^{(n,a)}-w_{k\mid a,s}r_{s}^{(n,a)}\|_{2}^{2}\right] (85)

where ek(n,a)=u¯k(n)−u¯a(n)e_{k}^{(n,a)}=\bar{u}_{k}^{(n)}-\bar{u}_{a}^{(n)} and rs(n,a)=u¯s(n)−u¯a(n)r_{s}^{(n,a)}=\bar{u}_{s}^{(n)}-\bar{u}_{a}^{(n)}.

For each candidate set 𝒞\mathcal{C}, top-1 agreement compares the maximizers of RlocalR_{\mathrm{local}} and GfixedG_{\mathrm{fixed}}, while normalized regret is 1−Gfixed​(slocal)/maxs∈𝒞⁡Gfixed​(s)1-G_{\mathrm{fixed}}(s_{\mathrm{local}})/\max_{s\in\mathcal{C}}G_{\mathrm{fixed}}(s).

C.2 Calibration Size and Selector Robustness

PoSTCache estimates the cross-timestep covariance kernel from a small set of offline denoising trajectories. Since the kernel is computed from deviations around the empirical mean, a single trajectory yields a degenerate zero covariance and cannot provide a meaningful uncertainty estimate. We therefore vary the calibration size from N=2N=2 to N=20N=20 and examine its effect on anchor selection and reconstruction fidelity.

As shown in Table 8, using only two trajectories leads to a less reliable covariance estimate and slightly lower reconstruction quality. Performance stabilizes from N=5N=5: using N=5N=5 and N=10N=10 produces identical schedules and reconstruction results, while increasing the calibration set to N=20N=20 provides no further improvement. These results indicate that the selected anchors are robust to the calibration size once a small number of trajectories is available. We use N=10N=10 throughout the main experiments as a conservative default that balances estimation reliability and offline profiling cost.

C.3 Schedule-Level Validation of the PVR Objective

The derivation in Sec. A.4 motivates PVR as a schedule-level surrogate: for an anchor set AA, the weighted posterior uncertainty

JPVR​(A):=∑t=1Tγt​Vt​(A)J_{\mathrm{PVR}}(A):=\sum_{t=1}^{T}\gamma_{t}V_{t}(A) (86)

should be small when the selected anchors provide informative future evidence for the remaining trajectory. We directly test this interpretation by asking whether JPVR​(A)J_{\mathrm{PVR}}(A) predicts the correction quality of complete anchor schedules on held-out trajectories. Our default selector greedily optimizes the global PVR objective by selecting the candidate with the largest marginal variance reduction over the full trajectory; we denote it as PVR (ours) below.

Protocol.

We evaluate Qwen-Image-2512 and Wan 2.1 using the Slow configurations in Tables 4 and 5. The proposal, scheduler-aware temporal weights, and postdictive correction follow Sec. B.2. For each model, the covariance kernel is constructed from the same 1010 calibration trajectories used by the selector and evaluated on 1616 held-out prompt–seed pairs. Their prompts, seeds, and exact prompt–seed combinations do not overlap with calibration.

Under a fixed computation budget, we evaluate 135135 unique schedules: 100100 randomly generated schedules, 3030 local perturbations of PVR (ours), and five named selectors—PVR (ours), preceding-interval PVR, local proposal risk, fixed interval, and distance only. Random schedules keep the dense prefix and final anchor fixed and sample the remaining anchor indices without replacement. Each local perturbation moves one non-mandatory PVR anchor by one to three timestep indices; collisions and out-of-range moves are rejected. The primary schedule pool uses seed 20260727.

For schedule AA, let u~k(n,A)\widetilde{u}_{k}^{(n,A)} and u^k(n,A)\widehat{u}_{k}^{(n,A)} denote the nearest-reuse proposal and its corrected prediction for held-out trajectory nn. Using the full-computation prediction u¯k(n)\bar{u}_{k}^{(n)} from Eq. (53), we measure

Epre​(A)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{pre}}(A) =1Nval​D​∑n=1Nval∑k∈𝒦evalγk​‖u¯k(n)−u~k(n,A)‖22,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{val}}D}\sum_{n=1}^{N_{\mathrm{val}}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{eval}}}\gamma_{k}\left\|\bar{u}_{k}^{(n)}-\widetilde{u}_{k}^{(n,A)}\right\|_{2}^{2}, (87)
Epost​(A)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{post}}(A) =1Nval​D​∑n=1Nval∑k∈𝒦evalγk​‖u¯k(n)−u^k(n,A)‖22,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{val}}D}\sum_{n=1}^{N_{\mathrm{val}}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{eval}}}\gamma_{k}\left\|\bar{u}_{k}^{(n)}-\widehat{u}_{k}^{(n,A)}\right\|_{2}^{2}, (88)

where 𝒦eval\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{eval}} contains all solver steps except the initial mandatory anchor, and DD is the product of all non-batch and non-temporal prediction dimensions. Right anchors are included in EpreE_{\mathrm{pre}} and have zero residual in EpostE_{\mathrm{post}}. We further define

QPVR​(A)=JPVR​(A0)−JPVR​(A),Rcorr​(A)=Epre​(A)−Epost​(A)Epre​(A),Q_{\mathrm{PVR}}(A)=J_{\mathrm{PVR}}(A_{0})-J_{\mathrm{PVR}}(A),\qquad R_{\mathrm{corr}}(A)=\frac{E_{\mathrm{pre}}(A)-E_{\mathrm{post}}(A)}{E_{\mathrm{pre}}(A)}, (89)

where A0A_{0} contains the mandatory anchors.

Schedule-level correspondence.

Figure 6 shows a clear monotonic relationship between predicted residual uncertainty and measured post-smoothing error: schedules with smaller JPVR​(A)J_{\mathrm{PVR}}(A) are generally concentrated in the lower-error region. The trend is particularly tight on Wan, whereas Qwen-Image exhibits greater dispersion among random schedules, indicating that its realized correction error contains additional variation not fully captured by the timestep-level covariance surrogate. Nevertheless, the overall ranking remains strong on both models.

The named selectors provide a complementary view. PVR (ours) lies in the most favorable lower-left region of both panels and achieves the lowest EpostE_{\mathrm{post}} among the named schedules. The local perturbations remain near the selected solution but generally move coherently upward and to the right, showing that the surrogate remains informative even among schedules with similar global structure.

These visual trends agree with Table 9. The Spearman correlation between JPVRJ_{\mathrm{PVR}} and EpostE_{\mathrm{post}} reaches 0.8580.858 on Qwen-Image and 0.9630.963 on Wan. Pairwise ranking accuracy, computed over all 90459045 unordered schedule pairs, is 83.7%83.7\% and 92.3%92.3\%, respectively; no ties occur in the primary pools. PVR (ours) outperforms 95.6%95.6\% and 97.8%97.8\% of the sampled schedules in terms of EpostE_{\mathrm{post}}, and outperforms all 100100 randomly generated schedules on both models.

Controlling for interval geometry.

To test whether the observed relationship is explained only by spacing, we define a schedule as gap matched when its maximum gap differs from PVR (ours) by at most 22 steps and the population standard deviation of its gaps differs by at most 0.750.75. This yields 6666 schedules on Qwen-Image and 7575 on Wan. We also compute partial rank correlations by regressing the average ranks of both variables on the average ranks of maximum gap and gap standard deviation.

The geometry-only correlations are notably weaker than the corresponding PVR correlations. The relationship remains strong within the gap-matched pools and after removing the rank-level effects of maximum gap and gap dispersion. Moreover, correction reduces the prediction-space error for all 2160=135×162160=135\times 16 schedule–trajectory pairs on each model. These results indicate that PVR captures schedule information beyond simple interval geometry.

Stability and scope.

Repeating schedule generation with seeds 20260728, 20260729, and 20260730 gives ρ⁡(JPVR,Epost)\rho(J_{\mathrm{PVR}},E_{\mathrm{post}}) ranges of 0.8600.860–0.8900.890 on Qwen-Image and 0.9620.962–0.9810.981 on Wan, with PVR (ours) percentiles of 94.8%94.8\%–97.0%97.0\% and 97.0%97.0\%–98.5%98.5\%, respectively. Thus, the main conclusions are stable to schedule-pool construction.

The confidence intervals in Table 9 are obtained from 10001000 paired bootstrap replicates using seed 20260728, resampling held-out trajectories while keeping the schedule pool fixed. They therefore quantify uncertainty across validation trajectories rather than schedule-pool sampling. Finally, this experiment is an offline prediction-space analysis on stored full-computation trajectories and does not model the closed-loop effect of reintegration on subsequent predictions. End-to-end behavior is evaluated separately by the online component ablations in Sec. 4.3.

C.4 Transferability of Offline PVR Schedules

PoSTCache estimates its cross-timestep dependency profile from a small set of offline denoising trajectories and uses the resulting PVR schedule for subsequent inference. We examine whether a schedule profiled in one setting can be reused after changing the prompt distribution, guidance scale, or spatial configuration, without collecting a new target calibration set.

For each target setting, we compare two schedules. Transferred directly reuses the schedule selected in the source setting, whereas Reprofiled recomputes the dependency profile from ten target calibration trajectories and reruns the same greedy PVR selector. Both schedules use the same full-computation budget, nearest-reuse proposal, and postdictive smoothing procedure. Each target setting is evaluated against its own full-inference reference.

We report the post-smoothing prediction error Epost​(A)E_{\mathrm{post}}(A) defined in Eq. 88, evaluated on target trajectories disjoint from calibration. This metric measures the discrepancy between corrected model predictions and their full-computation counterparts before accounting for the recursive effect of trajectory reintegration. We additionally report LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR against target full inference to measure the final closed-loop reconstruction quality.

Prompt-distribution transfer.

We first study FLUX.1-dev with 50 sampling steps and a full-computation budget of B=16B=16. The source schedule is profiled using the original calibration prompts and then transferred to PartiPrompts-Complex (Yu et al., 2022), whose prompts contain more challenging compositional relationships. Target reprofiling uses ten PartiPrompts-Complex calibration trajectories, while prediction-space evaluation uses ten disjoint held-out trajectories. End-to-end reconstruction is evaluated on 93 target prompts.

As shown in Table 11, target-specific reprofiling reduces EpostE_{\mathrm{post}}, indicating that its selected anchors better match the held-out target trajectories in prediction space. However, the transferred schedule is better on all three final reconstruction metrics. Paired bootstrap intervals over evaluation prompts exclude zero for LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR, showing that the final reconstruction advantage is not caused by a small number of prompts.

The source and target dependency profiles nevertheless remain highly similar, with a profile-similarity score of 0.9890.989. This suggests that the temporal structure exploited by PVR is largely preserved under the prompt shift. The disagreement between EpostE_{\mathrm{post}} and the final metrics also highlights the scope of Eq. 88: it measures prediction correction on stored target trajectories but does not fully capture how the corrected states alter subsequent denoising predictions after reintegration.

Guidance-scale transfer.

We next evaluate Qwen-Image-2512 by profiling the source schedule at CFG =4=4 and transferring it to CFG =2=2 and CFG =6=6. All configurations use 50 sampling steps, B=16B=16, the same negative prompt, and identical prompt–seed splits. For each target CFG, ten trajectories are used for target reprofiling, ten disjoint trajectories are used to evaluate EpostE_{\mathrm{post}}, and 50 prompts are used for end-to-end reconstruction.

Table 12 reveals different behaviors at the two target guidance scales. At CFG =2=2, reprofiling substantially reduces EpostE_{\mathrm{post}}. The original target-reprofiled schedule also performs well relative to schedules obtained by resampling the target calibration set, indicating that the prediction-space improvement is reproducible rather than an accidental schedule choice. Nevertheless, paired-bootstrap intervals for LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR all include zero. Thus, adapting the profile improves the prediction-space criterion but does not produce a statistically distinguishable improvement in final reconstruction. This is the clearest case in which EpostE_{\mathrm{post}} is informative but incomplete as a proxy for the closed-loop trajectory.

At CFG =6=6, the transferred schedule instead obtains lower EpostE_{\mathrm{post}} and better mean reconstruction metrics. The LPIPS improvement is supported by a paired-bootstrap interval excluding zero, whereas the SSIM and PSNR differences are less conclusive. Additional cross-evaluation shows that the target-reprofiled schedule is favored by the profile constructed from its calibration trajectories but becomes worse when scored using independent target trajectories.

Spatial-configuration transfer.

Finally, we profile a Qwen-Image-2512 schedule at 1328×13281328\times 1328 and reuse it at 1024×10241024\times 1024 and 1664×9281664\times 928. The first target changes the resolution while preserving the square aspect ratio. The second additionally changes the aspect ratio and spatial token-grid geometry. The guidance scale, sampling steps, full-computation budget, prompts, negative prompt, and profiling procedure are otherwise kept unchanged.

For the resolution-only shift to 1024×10241024\times 1024, target reprofiling slightly improves EpostE_{\mathrm{post}} and LPIPS, whereas the transferred schedule obtains higher SSIM and PSNR. The corresponding held-out PVR scores are nearly identical, showing that the two schedules are practically comparable.

For the wider 1664×9281664\times 928 configuration, the transferred schedule is clearly better in both prediction and reconstruction space. Meanwhile, the source–target profile similarity remains as high as 0.9960.996, indicating that the underlying temporal dependency structures differ only modestly. Despite this limited profile shift, the two resulting schedules produce substantially different EpostE_{\mathrm{post}} values and final reconstruction quality. This disproportionate effect suggests a limitation of the discrete greedy selector: small perturbations in the estimated profile can change early anchor choices, which in turn alter subsequent conditional gains and lead to markedly different complete schedules. The result therefore highlights the path dependence and finite-sample instability of greedy anchor selection, rather than a large structural difference between the source and target profiles.

Results analysis.

The experiments above show that target-specific reprofiling may improve, match, or underperform direct transfer. To identify where these differences arise, we use three complementary diagnostics.

First, profile similarity measures whether the source and target settings exhibit similar relative cross-timestep dependency patterns. Let K(s)K^{(s)} and K(t)K^{(t)} denote the covariance kernels estimated from the source and target calibration trajectories, respectively, using Eq. 100. Since their marginal prediction variances may differ across settings, we first convert each covariance kernel into a correlation profile:

Ci​j(x)=Ki​j(x)max⁡(Ki​i(x),ϵ)​max⁡(Kj​j(x),ϵ),x∈{s,t},C^{(x)}_{ij}=\frac{K^{(x)}_{ij}}{\sqrt{\max\!\left(K^{(x)}_{ii},\epsilon\right)\max\!\left(K^{(x)}_{jj},\epsilon\right)}},\qquad x\in\{s,t\}, (90)

where ϵ=10−12\epsilon=10^{-12} is used for numerical stability.

Let

𝐜(x)=veci<j⁡(Ci​j(x))\mathbf{c}^{(x)}=\operatorname{vec}_{i<j}\left(C^{(x)}_{ij}\right) (91)

denote the vector containing the strictly upper-triangular entries of C(x)C^{(x)}. We define profile similarity as the Pearson correlation between the source and target profile vectors:

Simprofile=∑k(ck(s)−c¯(s))​(ck(t)−c¯(t))∑k(ck(s)−c¯(s))2​∑k(ck(t)−c¯(t))2.\operatorname{Sim}_{\mathrm{profile}}=\frac{\sum_{k}\left(c_{k}^{(s)}-\bar{c}^{(s)}\right)\left(c_{k}^{(t)}-\bar{c}^{(t)}\right)}{\sqrt{\sum_{k}\left(c_{k}^{(s)}-\bar{c}^{(s)}\right)^{2}}\sqrt{\sum_{k}\left(c_{k}^{(t)}-\bar{c}^{(t)}\right)^{2}}}. (92)

The diagonal is excluded because it is one after correlation normalization, and only the upper triangle is retained to avoid counting each symmetric timestep pair twice. A value close to one indicates that the source and target profiles exhibit similar relative cross-timestep dependency patterns, even when their absolute covariance magnitudes or marginal variances differ.

Second, we cross-evaluate the two fixed schedules using an independent target profile and report which one obtains the lower schedule-level uncertainty JPVR​(A)J_{\mathrm{PVR}}(A) from Eq. 86. This checks whether an advantage on the target calibration profile persists beyond the trajectories used to construct it.

Third, we assess sensitivity to the particular ten target calibration trajectories. We repeatedly resample these trajectories with replacement, recompute the target profile, and rerun greedy schedule selection. Each bootstrap schedule is then evaluated on the same target held-out trajectories using EpostE_{\mathrm{post}} from Eq. 88. The target-schedule percentile is the fraction of these bootstrap schedules outperformed by the original target-reprofiled schedule. A high percentile means that the reported target schedule is typical or relatively strong among schedules obtained from the same target setting, whereas a low percentile indicates an unfavorable calibration or greedy-selection realization.

Table 14 separates three qualitatively different cases. For prompt OOD, the two dependency profiles are nearly identical and the original target schedule lies near the middle of its bootstrap distribution. The reprofiled schedule has lower held-out JPVRJ_{\mathrm{PVR}} and EpostE_{\mathrm{post}}, but worse final reconstruction. The result is therefore best interpreted as strong profile overlap together with a fixed-schedule mismatch between prediction-space ranking and closed-loop output quality.

At CFG =2=2, the target schedule has lower held-out JPVRJ_{\mathrm{PVR}}, lower EpostE_{\mathrm{post}}, and a high bootstrap percentile. Target adaptation is therefore consistently beneficial for the prediction-space objective, even though the final images remain statistically indistinguishable. In contrast, the target schedules at CFG =6=6 and 1664×9281664\times 928 have low bootstrap percentiles and are also worse under the independent target profile. Their poor final results do not indicate that source profiles are intrinsically superior. Instead, estimating a profile from a finite calibration split and applying discrete greedy selection can produce an unfavorable target schedule. The 1024×10241024\times 1024 case lies between these regimes: target reprofiling slightly improves the prediction-space metrics, while the two schedules remain effectively comparable in final reconstruction.

Overall, the source PVR schedule remains a robust practical default across the evaluated prompt, guidance, and spatial shifts. These results do not imply that the dependency profile is invariant or that target adaptation is generally harmful. Rather, target reprofiling can provide genuine prediction-space improvements, but these improvements need not translate into better reintegrated outputs. This discrepancy reflects the current offline–online gap: the offline PVR objective and EpostE_{\mathrm{post}} are evaluated on stored full-computation trajectories, whereas online reintegration changes the latent states and recursively affects all subsequent model predictions. In addition, finite-sample profile estimation with greedy selection can introduce further variability into discrete anchor selection.

C.5 Additional Ablation Studies

Temporal weighting.

We ablate the power pp in the scheduler-aware temporal weight

γ~t=(medianj⁡δjδt+ϵ)p.\widetilde{\gamma}_{t}=\left(\frac{\operatorname{median}_{j}\delta_{j}}{\delta_{t}+\epsilon}\right)^{p}. (93)

Setting p=0p=0 yields uniform weighting, while larger values place greater emphasis on densely sampled scheduler regions. We conduct this ablation on Qwen-Image-2512 with budget_steps=16\texttt{budget\_steps}=16 and dense_prefix=7\texttt{dense\_prefix}=7, keeping the clipping range and all other configurations fixed.

As shown in Table 15, the default setting p=0.5p=0.5 achieves the best overall reconstruction fidelity, reducing LPIPS from 0.0632 to 0.0607 and improving SSIM from 0.9262 to 0.9302 and PSNR from 26.781 to 27.597 compared with uniform weighting. Larger powers provide no further improvement, suggesting that excessively emphasizing densely sampled regions is not beneficial. We therefore use p=0.5p=0.5 in the main experiments.

Mandatory prefix anchors.

We study the effect of the dense-prefix length while fixing the total full-computation budget. Specifically, we evaluate FLUX.1-dev with budget_steps=16\texttt{budget\_steps}=16 and vary the number of consecutive full-computation steps at the beginning of the sampling trajectory. Since the total budget is fixed, increasing the dense-prefix length allocates more anchors to the early denoising stage while leaving fewer anchors for PVR-based selection over the remaining trajectory.

As shown in Table 16, reconstruction quality first improves and then degrades as the dense-prefix length increases. A short prefix leaves the rapidly varying early denoising stage insufficiently covered, whereas an overly long prefix consumes too much of the fixed budget and limits adaptive anchor placement over the remaining trajectory. The default setting of 77 achieves the best performance across all three metrics, reducing LPIPS to 0.09680.0968 while increasing SSIM and PSNR to 0.89440.8944 and 26.28426.284, respectively.

The optimal dense-prefix length depends on the model, scheduler, and total budget, and does not admit a simple closed-form prescription. We therefore adopt the empirical rule

Lprefix∈{⌊ℬ2⌋−1,⌊ℬ2⌋},L_{\mathrm{prefix}}\in\left\{\left\lfloor\frac{\mathcal{B}}{2}\right\rfloor-1,\,\left\lfloor\frac{\mathcal{B}}{2}\right\rfloor\right\}, (94)

which is used for all model-specific configurations reported in Table 5.

Comparison with DPCache.

PVR globally models cross-timestep dependencies when evaluating the information value of an anchor. DPCache (Cui et al., 2026) is therefore the closest conceptual comparison, as it also formulates timestep selection as a global optimization problem, but minimizes a path-additive cost through dynamic programming.

To isolate the scheduling objective, we adapt DPCache to the same PoSTCache online pipeline. DPCache-Pre follows the original pre-correction principle and constructs its path cost from nearest-reuse proposal errors before postdictive smoothing. DPCache-Retro is our correction-aware extension, which retains the same dynamic-programming formulation but computes the interval cost after applying postdictive smoothing. All selectors use FLUX.1-dev with 50 sampling steps, a budget of B=16B=16, ten calibration trajectories, and the same nearest-reuse and single-anchor smoothing pipeline. Prediction-space evaluation uses ten disjoint held-out trajectories, while reconstruction metrics are evaluated over 200 prompts.

As shown in Table 17, DPCache-Retro consistently improves over DPCache-Pre, confirming that anchor scheduling should account for the subsequent postdictive correction. DPCache-Retro obtains a slightly lower held-out EpostE_{\mathrm{post}} than PVR, which is expected because its path cost is directly constructed from the post-smoothing prediction error. Nevertheless, PVR achieves the best final reconstruction quality across all three metrics.

This discrepancy further reflects the offline–online gap: reducing prediction error on stored full-computation trajectories does not fully capture how reintegration changes the latent trajectory and recursively affects later model predictions. It also highlights the distinction between the two global objectives: DPCache minimizes fixed path-additive interval costs, whereas PVR evaluates the uncertainty reduction of each anchor conditioned on the complete selected set, thereby modeling redundancy and complementarity among anchors.

C.6 Anchor-State Consistency and Compute Allocation

Local anchor-state consistency.

At a future anchor bb, the full prediction used to construct the anchor innovation is evaluated at the state x~b\widetilde{x}_{b} reached by the forward proposal trajectory. Postdictive smoothing subsequently revises the preceding skipped predictions and reintegrates the interval from anchor aa, yielding a corrected anchor state x^b\widehat{x}_{b}. Because the default implementation retains the already-computed anchor prediction, it is not re-evaluated at x^b\widehat{x}_{b}. To quantify the resulting local state–prediction mismatch, we compare

u¯b=fθ​(x~b,τb),ubfresh=fθ​(x^b,τb),\bar{u}_{b}=f_{\theta}(\widetilde{x}_{b},\tau_{b}),\qquad u_{b}^{\mathrm{fresh}}=f_{\theta}(\widehat{x}_{b},\tau_{b}), (95)

where ubfreshu_{b}^{\mathrm{fresh}} is used only as a diagnostic probe and does not alter the default sampling trajectory.

We measure the relative state displacement and prediction discrepancy as

Dx​(b)=‖x^b−x~b‖2‖x~b‖2,Eanchor​(b)=‖ubfresh−u¯b‖2‖ubfresh‖2.D_{x}(b)=\frac{\|\widehat{x}_{b}-\widetilde{x}_{b}\|_{2}}{\|\widetilde{x}_{b}\|_{2}},\qquad E_{\mathrm{anchor}}(b)=\frac{\|u_{b}^{\mathrm{fresh}}-\bar{u}_{b}\|_{2}}{\|u_{b}^{\mathrm{fresh}}\|_{2}}. (96)

We additionally report the directional discrepancy

Canchor​(b)=1−cos⁡(ubfresh,u¯b).C_{\mathrm{anchor}}(b)=1-\cos\left(u_{b}^{\mathrm{fresh}},\bar{u}_{b}\right). (97)

To assess whether this prediction discrepancy materially affects the subsequent numerical update, we further define

Estep​(b)=‖𝒮b​(x^b,u¯b,τb)−𝒮b​(x^b,ubfresh,τb)‖2‖𝒮b​(x^b,ubfresh,τb)‖2.E_{\mathrm{step}}(b)=\frac{\left\|\mathcal{S}_{b}\left(\widehat{x}_{b},\bar{u}_{b},\tau_{b}\right)-\mathcal{S}_{b}\left(\widehat{x}_{b},u_{b}^{\mathrm{fresh}},\tau_{b}\right)\right\|_{2}}{\left\|\mathcal{S}_{b}\left(\widehat{x}_{b},u_{b}^{\mathrm{fresh}},\tau_{b}\right)\right\|_{2}}. (98)

We conduct this diagnostic analysis on Qwen-Image-2512 and Wan 2.1 using their Fast and Slow configurations in Table 5. We use eight evaluation prompts with a fixed random seed and identical prompt–seed pairs across all compared variants. All consistency statistics are averaged over the cache intervals encountered during inference.

As shown in Table 18, reintegration changes the future-anchor state only modestly, with Dx<2.3%D_{x}<2.3\% across all evaluated settings. The resulting prediction discrepancy is measurable, whereas the normalized downstream state discrepancy after one solver update is approximately one order of magnitude smaller. Qwen-Image exhibits nearly unchanged consistency statistics between its Fast and Slow configurations, while Wan shows a larger discrepancy under the sparser Fast schedule. Furthermore, DxD_{x} and EanchorE_{\mathrm{anchor}} are strongly correlated (Spearman ρ=0.845\rho=0.845–0.9250.925), as are EanchorE_{\mathrm{anchor}} and EstepE_{\mathrm{step}} (ρ=0.892\rho=0.892–0.9170.917). These results support the expected propagation from reintegration-induced state displacement to prediction staleness and subsequently to the numerical solver update, while showing that the immediate downstream perturbation remains comparatively small.

Fresh-anchor oracle and compute allocation.

A small discrepancy after a single numerical update does not necessarily imply negligible end-to-end impact, since diffusion sampling recursively feeds each updated latent state into subsequent model evaluations. We therefore construct a Fresh-Anchor Oracle that recomputes the model prediction at the reintegrated anchor state and uses this fresh prediction for subsequent sampling. Importantly, the preceding cache interval is not smoothed or reintegrated a second time, so this variant isolates the effect of restoring anchor-state consistency rather than introducing an additional correction iteration.

Fresh-anchor recomputation consistently improves reconstruction relative to the corresponding Fast configuration, reducing LPIPS from 0.07490.0749 to 0.05530.0553 on Qwen-Image and from 0.09140.0914 to 0.07670.0767 on Wan. This confirms that the local state–prediction mismatch, although small at each individual solver update, can accumulate into a measurable end-to-end reconstruction gap.

Restoring exact consistency, however, requires additional neural-network evaluations. To determine whether anchor refresh is an effective use of this extra computation, we perform an NFE-matched comparison on Qwen-Image. Its Fast configuration uses ℬ=14\mathcal{B}=14 and a dense-prefix length Lprefix=7L_{\mathrm{prefix}}=7. The Fresh-Anchor Oracle retains these seven dense-prefix evaluations and refreshes all seven post-prefix anchors, including the mandatory final anchor, resulting in 14+7=2114+7=21 total NFEs.

For the compute-matched baseline, we instead set ℬ=21\mathcal{B}=21 and Lprefix=10L_{\mathrm{prefix}}=10 and rerun the same PVR anchor selection procedure. Thus, both variants use exactly 2121 model evaluations, but spend the additional computation differently: the Fresh-Anchor Oracle re-evaluates already-selected anchors, whereas the standard ℬ=21\mathcal{B}=21 configuration allocates the evaluations to broader temporal anchor coverage.

At the identical budget of 2121 NFEs, broader anchor coverage reduces LPIPS from 0.05530.0553 to 0.02390.0239, while improving SSIM from 0.96220.9622 to 0.98010.9801 and PSNR from 30.9730.97 to 34.0434.04. Hence, although explicit anchor refresh reveals genuine consistency headroom, the same additional model evaluations are substantially more effective when allocated to informative new anchors in this controlled Qwen-Image comparison.

The Wan operating points provide complementary evidence. Fresh-anchor recomputation improves the Fast configuration from LPIPS 0.09140.0914 to 0.07670.0767, but requires 2424 NFEs and still remains slightly behind the 2020-NFE Slow configuration with LPIPS 0.07170.0717. Together, these results show that unconditional anchor refresh is not an obviously preferable use of additional computation. In the controlled Qwen-Image comparison, allocating the same NFE budget to broader anchor coverage is substantially more effective, while Wan exhibits the same qualitative tendency despite using different operating points. This supports our default design of prioritizing informative temporal anchors without introducing mandatory refresh evaluations.

C.7 Efficiency and Runtime Analysis

Offline calibration cost.

PoSTCache uses complete denoising trajectories to estimate the cross-timestep covariance kernel, but the raw high-dimensional predictions do not need to be persistently stored. For each calibration trajectory Z(n)∈ℝT×DZ^{(n)}\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times D}, we accumulate the sufficient statistics

S=∑n=1NZ(n),Q=∑n=1NZ(n)​Z(n)⊤,S=\sum_{n=1}^{N}Z^{(n)},\qquad Q=\sum_{n=1}^{N}Z^{(n)}Z^{(n)\top}, (99)

from which the kernel used by the PVR selector is recovered exactly as

K=QN​D−S​S⊤N2​D.K=\frac{Q}{ND}-\frac{SS^{\top}}{N^{2}D}. (100)

Therefore, each trajectory can be discarded immediately after its contribution has been accumulated. This procedure reduces offline data-loading and repeated-processing overhead and substantially decreases the storage footprint, while exactly preserving all information required by the current PVR selector.

As shown in Table 20, collecting ten calibration trajectories takes 5.05 minutes on Qwen-Image-2512 and 11.12 minutes on Wan 2.1. Streaming kernel construction adds only 2.96 seconds and 14.43 seconds, corresponding to approximately 1.0% and 2.2% of the respective collection time. The dominant offline cost therefore remains the N complete denoising runs rather than covariance accumulation. This cost is paid only once per model and sampling configuration, after which the resulting kernel and anchor schedule are shared across all subsequent inference runs.

After applying the sufficient-statistics compression, the persistent selector state is reduced from 0.411–1.953 GiB of raw predictions to approximately 22 KiB, as its dominant component scales with T2T^{2} rather than N​T​DNTD. The serialized artifact additionally contains temporal weights and configuration metadata, much of which can be readily reconstructed from the sampling configuration at runtime; retaining only the covariance kernel would further reduce the storage footprint. Once the kernel and selector configuration are available in memory, constructing a complete anchor schedule takes only 3.47–3.74 ms in median. This schedule-construction cost is incurred only once for each model and sampling configuration, after which the resulting schedule is stored and reused during inference, and therefore does not contribute to per-sample online latency.

Online inference overhead.

Postdictive smoothing requires only lightweight vector operations and scheduler reintegration, without introducing additional neural-network evaluations at skipped timesteps. Table 21 reports the runtime breakdown on Wan 2.1 with a full-computation budget of 20 steps and a dense prefix of 10 steps. We separately measure the costs of neural-network evaluations, postdictive correction and orchestration, scheduler reintegration, VAE decoding, and pipeline preparation. The correction and reintegration together account for only 0.21% of the total latency, indicating that the computational overhead introduced by PoSTCache is negligible.

Efficiency–quality trade-off.

Figure 7 further reports the complete quality–latency trade-off using all three reconstruction metrics. Across 1-LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR, PoSTCache consistently dominates the corresponding caching baseline over a broad range of latency budgets.

C.8 Additional Qualitative Results

We provide additional qualitative comparisons to complement the image results in the main paper. The examples cover diverse prompts, model architectures, and acceleration regimes. Across these settings, PoSTCache more closely follows full inference in terms of global composition, local appearance, and object structure. For video generation, it additionally reduces structural and appearance deviations across the sampled frames, while achieving acceleration ratios comparable to or higher than those of the competing methods.

Qwen-Image-2512.

Figure 8 presents additional text-to-image results on Qwen-Image-2512. At a 2.90×2.90\times speedup, PoSTCache closely preserves both the global layout and fine-grained structures of full inference. In the fireworks example, it retains the shapes of the rendered letters and the local burst patterns. In the moonlit cat and industrial landscape examples, it better preserves small foreground elements, cloud boundaries, vegetation, and reflection details. In comparison, competing methods tend to smooth away these local structures or introduce more noticeable changes in color, illumination, and scene layout. These results indicate that postdictive correction mitigates not only semantic degradation but also the accumulation of fine-grained appearance errors.

OpenSora 1.2.

Figure 9 compares PoSTCache with representative caching methods on OpenSora 1.2. PoSTCache more faithfully preserves object identity, geometry, and prompt-specified spatial relationships across the sampled frames. For example, it maintains the contour and proportions of the pink vase, the relative arrangement of the couch and bed, and the left–right relationship between the toothbrush and hair drier. TeaCache and MagCache, by contrast, produce more visible changes in object shape, orientation, or relative placement. The improvements are obtained at a comparable acceleration ratio, suggesting that retrospective correction is effective for preventing structural deviations from propagating along the video trajectory.

CogVideoX.

Figure 10 further evaluates PoSTCache on CogVideoX using stylized landscapes, natural scenes, and architectural objects. PoSTCache closely reproduces the object scale and scene composition of full inference, including the position of the Eiffel Tower and boat, the appearance of the lakeside bench, and the silhouette of the Gothic-style lamppost. Moreover, these structures remain comparatively stable across the displayed frames. TeaCache and SenCache exhibit larger variations in object proportions, background layout, or foreground appearance. This comparison demonstrates that PoSTCache remains effective when the underlying model architecture and visual content differ substantially from those of OpenSora.

Wan 2.1.

Figure 11 shows the corresponding comparisons on Wan 2.1. The selected prompts test both compositional relationships and the preservation of distinctive scene structures. For the boat–airplane example, PoSTCache maintains the prompt-specified relative positions and closely follows the full-inference object silhouettes. For the lighthouse and castle examples, it preserves the principal architectural structures, surrounding vegetation, and overall scene appearance across frames. DiCache introduces substantial structural degradation in the lighthouse scene, while SenCache produces more noticeable changes in object geometry and background appearance. PoSTCache therefore provides a closer approximation to full inference while attaining the highest acceleration ratio among the compared methods in this setting.

Overall, the qualitative results are consistent with the reconstruction metrics reported in the main paper. By revising skipped predictions using future-anchor evidence, PoSTCache reduces accumulated errors in local texture, object geometry, spatial composition, and temporal appearance across different image and video generation architectures.

C.9 Limitations and Boundary Conditions

PoSTCache relies on offline trajectory statistics to construct a shared anchor schedule. The resulting schedule transfers well across the evaluated prompt distributions, guidance scales, and spatial configurations, but this does not imply that the underlying dependency profile is invariant or that a single schedule is optimal for every sample. Target-specific reprofiling can improve the offline PVR objective or the held-out prediction-space error without improving the final reconstruction. This discrepancy reflects an offline–online gap: the offline profile is estimated on stored full-computation trajectories, whereas online correction changes the latent states and recursively affects subsequent model predictions. In addition, the current greedy selector is path dependent; small finite-sample perturbations of otherwise similar covariance profiles can alter early anchor choices and produce substantially different schedules. Combining the shared offline prior with inexpensive online trajectory observations is therefore a promising direction for more stable and sample-adaptive anchor selection.

Retrospective reintegration can also introduce a local state–prediction mismatch at future anchors. Appendix C.6 shows that unconditional anchor refresh reduces this mismatch but is less compute-efficient than broader anchor coverage in our matched-NFE comparison. Our analysis nevertheless compares only two coarse allocation strategies and does not exclude more selective policies. An adaptive scheme that refreshes only high-risk anchors, or dynamically allocates each additional model evaluation between anchor refresh and new anchor placement, may yield a more favorable consistency–coverage trade-off.

Postdictive correction further relies on the temporal correlation between skipped prediction errors and innovations revealed by future anchors. Our implementation approximates the full covariance-dependent smoothing gain with an isotropic linear gain determined by sampling progress. Although this approximation is effective in the evaluated regimes, it cannot fully capture nonlinear, feature-dependent, or sample-specific error evolution. Under very aggressive acceleration or unusually long cache intervals, accumulated drift may weaken the relationship between a future innovation and earlier skipped predictions, limiting the recoverable error.
